title: About me
text:
I am a PhD student at the University of Liverpool, interested in how the smallest pieces of genetic information can shape bacterial behaviour and evolution.
My previous projects have explored plant connectivity, rhizobacteria and insect–plant interactions, and the genomic diversity of gut Clostridia.

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
text:
← All writing
The comparison is surprising. Bacterial plasmids and cancer-associated extrachromosomal DNA, or ecDNA, exist in completely different organisms and operate within very different cellular systems.
Yet both can replicate independently of chromosomes, exist at multiple copies within a cell and segregate imperfectly during cell division.1
Those properties make extrachromosomal DNA more than an alternative place to store genes. They can fundamentally alter how quickly populations generate variation and respond to selection.

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
section: Copy number changes what a gene can do
text:
Copy number changes what a gene can do
Moving a gene onto a multicopy element immediately changes its biological context.
A chromosomal gene may exist once per genome. The same gene carried on a plasmid can exist at tens or even hundreds of copies per cell.
For dose-dependent traits, that difference matters. Increasing the number of resistance-gene copies can increase the amount of resistance protein produced and therefore increase the level of resistance.
But copy number also changes the evolutionary potential of the gene.
More copies mean more DNA molecules on which mutations can occur. Experiments with multicopy plasmids have shown that this increased mutational supply can accelerate the evolution of antibiotic resistance.2
Recent work has also shown that plasmid copy number follows broader relationships with plasmid size, suggesting that copy number itself is a fundamental feature of plasmid ecology and evolution rather than simply a laboratory parameter.3

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
text:
Imperfect inheritance creates variation
Chromosomes are normally inherited with remarkable precision.
High-copy plasmids are less predictable.
When a bacterial cell divides, plasmid copies may not be distributed equally between its daughters. Over several generations, this creates a population containing cells with different plasmid copy numbers.
This variation can directly produce variation in phenotype.
Hernandez-Beltran and colleagues showed that variation in plasmid copy number can generate phenotypic noise in antibiotic resistance, creating transiently resistant cells within an otherwise genetically similar population.4
That has an important evolutionary consequence.
If the environment suddenly changes, some cells may already possess a plasmid copy number suited to the new conditions. Selection can therefore act immediately on variation that already exists within the population.
The same principle appears in cancer.
ecDNA lacks conventional chromosomal segregation machinery, meaning daughter cells can inherit different numbers of oncogene-carrying ecDNA molecules. This generates substantial variation within tumours and allows ecDNA abundance to respond rapidly to treatment.5

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
section: Evolution does not always have to wait for mutation
text:
Evolution does not always have to wait for mutation
This is perhaps the most interesting part of the analogy.
We often think about adaptation as:
mutation → selection → spread
Extrachromosomal DNA introduces another route:
copy-number variation → selection → rapid phenotypic change
A population can therefore alter the dosage of an existing gene without waiting for a new mutation to arise.
If selection changes again, the distribution of copy numbers can shift back.
The paper describes plasmids and ecDNA as potential contingency loci: unusually evolvable portions of the genome capable of generating phenotypic diversity when conditions change.1
This idea is particularly interesting for antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotic exposure is rarely constant. Bacteria experience pulses of selection as antibiotic concentrations rise and fall between environments, tissues and treatments.
A genetic system capable of rapidly generating both high- and low-copy subpopulations could provide considerable flexibility under those conditions.

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
section: Extrachromosomal DNA can reshape the rest of the cell
text:
Extrachromosomal DNA can reshape the rest of the cell
Copy number is only part of the story.
Plasmids can also alter bacterial phenotype by changing the expression of chromosomal genes.
Multidrug-resistance plasmids have been shown to reprogramme host transcription, including metabolic pathways that have no obvious direct relationship to the resistance genes carried by the plasmid.6
This raises a broader evolutionary question: why would a plasmid alter host behaviour?
One possibility is that some plasmid-induced phenotypes improve the persistence or transmission of the plasmid itself. This has led to the suggestion that plasmids can effectively manipulate bacterial phenotype, rather than functioning simply as passive vehicles for accessory genes.7
ecDNA provides an interesting parallel.
In cancer cells, different ecDNA molecules can physically associate into regulatory hubs, allowing enhancers and oncogenes carried on separate molecules to interact.8
Again, DNA outside the chromosome becomes part of the regulatory architecture of the cell.

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
section: Plasmids and ecDNA are not the same thing
text:
Plasmids and ecDNA are not the same thing
The analogy has limits.
Plasmids can move horizontally between bacterial cells and even between species. Their evolutionary interests can therefore become partly independent of the bacterium currently carrying them.
Cancer ecDNA generally remains within a tumour lineage.
Plasmids can also acquire genes from many evolutionary sources, whereas ecDNA originates from chromosomal DNA within the host cell.
The molecular mechanisms involved in replication and segregation are also very different.
The interesting similarity is therefore at the level of evolutionary function.
Despite their independent origins, both systems allow important genes to exist on autonomously replicating, variably inherited DNA molecules.1

title: Plasmids, ecDNA and the evolutionary power of DNA outside chromosomes
section: A different way to think about plasmids
text:
A different way to think about plasmids
Plasmid biology is often framed around horizontal gene transfer.
That makes sense, particularly when thinking about antimicrobial resistance.
But the comparison with ecDNA highlights another dimension of plasmid evolution: what happens after the plasmid arrives inside the cell?
Its copy number can change.
Its genes can mutate.
Its structure can rearrange.
Its inheritance can generate cell-to-cell variation.
And its presence can alter the expression and behaviour of the bacterial host.
For me, this connects directly with the questions behind my PhD.
If an antimicrobial-resistance plasmid changes bacterial behaviour, is that simply a physiological side effect of carrying additional DNA?
Is the bacterium adapting to the plasmid?
Or has selection shaped plasmids to modify their hosts in ways that improve plasmid persistence and transmission?
Thinking about plasmids as independent evolutionary entities makes those questions much more interesting.

title: Why plasmids are more than resistance vectors
text:
← All writing
That wider relationship is the starting point for my PhD at the University of Liverpool. I study how antimicrobial-resistance plasmids influence bacterial behaviour and evolution, with a focus on plasmid–host interactions in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

title: Why plasmids are more than resistance vectors
section: A gene is only part of the question
text:
A gene is only part of the question
When thinking about a resistance plasmid, it is natural to ask which resistance genes it carries. My research begins with a related question: what changes when a bacterium acquires the plasmid?
That question shifts attention towards the host. What happens to its phenotype? Does its social behaviour change? How does the relationship between plasmid and bacterium develop as they evolve together? These are the questions I want to investigate, rather than treating resistance as the only feature that matters.

title: Why plasmids are more than resistance vectors
section: Looking at behaviour and evolution together
text:
Looking at behaviour and evolution together
My project brings together bacterial phenotyping, microbial genetics, experimental evolution and quantitative analysis. Each offers a different way to examine the relationship between a plasmid and its host.
Phenotyping puts bacterial behaviour at the centre of the work. Experimental evolution adds the question of how that relationship changes over time. Together, these approaches frame the project around both the immediate effects of acquiring a plasmid and the longer-term dynamics of adaptation.
The aim is to understand the connection between mobile DNA, the cells that carry it and the ways bacteria adapt. This note sets out the questions motivating that work; the research itself is ongoing.
